title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Conditional Requests
summary: Defines HTTP/1.1 conditional requests: metadata header fields that describe state changes, request header fields that set preconditions, and the rules for responses when a precondition fails. It was later replaced by RFC 9110.

eli5.summary: A browser can ask, only send me this page if it changed since last time. This document explains how that question works so nothing is downloaded twice. It was later replaced.

questions: how do http conditional requests work
what is the lost update problem
subtitle: How HTTP clients ask 'only if it changed' and 'only if it is still the version I saw', using validators and preconditions.

tldr.problem: HTTP clients and caches need to avoid re-downloading unchanged data, and clients that change resources in parallel need to avoid overwriting each other's work.
tldr.mechanism: Servers label representations with validators (Last-Modified dates and ETag entity-tags). Clients echo them back in precondition headers (If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since, If-Range), and servers answer 304 Not Modified or 412 Precondition Failed when a condition is false.
tldr.outcome: Conditional GETs are the most efficient way to update HTTP caches, and conditional writes prevent the lost update problem. This RFC obsoleted RFC 2616 in part and was itself obsoleted by RFC 9110.

today: RFC 7232 is obsoleted by RFC 9110, which now defines HTTP semantics including conditional requests. It replaced part of RFC 2616 when published in June 2014.

sections.title: Conditional Requests
sections.content:
A conditional request is an HTTP request with one or more header fields stating a precondition that is tested before the method is applied to the target resource. RFC 7232 defines these mechanisms for HTTP/1.1.

The RFC names two main uses. Conditional GET requests are the most efficient mechanism for updating HTTP caches. Conditionals can also be applied to state-changing methods such as PUT and DELETE to prevent the lost update problem, where one client accidentally overwrites the work of another client acting in parallel.
sections.eli5: A conditional request is a request with a 'only if' attached. It saves repeat downloads and stops two people from accidentally erasing each other's changes.

sections.title: Validators: Last-Modified and ETag
sections.content:
Metadata used in a precondition is called a validator. The RFC defines two: modification dates and opaque entity tags.

Last-Modified is a timestamp of when the origin server believes the selected representation last changed. An origin server MUST NOT send a date later than its time of message origination. A Last-Modified time used as a validator is implicitly weak, unless for example it is at least 60 seconds before the Date value of the cached response.

ETag carries an entity-tag: an opaque quoted string, possibly prefixed with W/ to mark it weak. Examples are "xyzzy" and W/"xyzzy". The tag is opaque, so the client does not need to know how it was built; servers might use a revision number, a hash of the content, or a timestamp with sub-second resolution.

A strong validator changes whenever the representation data changes in a way visible in a 200 (OK) response to GET. A weak one might not, for example because of one-second clock resolution. Strong validators work for all conditional requests; weak ones only where exact equality with the earlier data is not needed, such as cache validation. An origin server SHOULD send an entity-tag and a Last-Modified value in successful GET or HEAD responses when feasible.

Two comparison functions exist. Strong comparison needs both tags to be non-weak with identical opaque values. Weak comparison ignores the weakness flag and compares the opaque values only.
sections.eli5: A validator is like a version sticker on a book. A strong sticker changes with every edit; a weak sticker may stay the same after a tiny edit.

sections.title: The Precondition Header Fields
sections.content:
Five request header fields carry preconditions:

  • If-Match: true when the current representation's entity-tag matches one in the list, or when any representation exists if the value is the wildcard value. It uses strong comparison and is mostly used with POST, PUT and DELETE to prevent lost updates. If false, the server MUST NOT perform the method and responds 412 (or a 2xx if the change is already reflected).
  • If-None-Match: true when no listed tag matches (or no representation exists, for the wildcard value). It uses weak comparison. It is mainly used in conditional GETs to update cached data. A false result gives 304 for GET or HEAD and 412 for other methods. With the wildcard value on a PUT it stops a client from overwriting a resource that already exists.
  • If-Modified-Since: makes a GET or HEAD conditional on the representation being modified after the given date. If it has not, the server SHOULD send 304. It is ignored if If-None-Match is present.
  • If-Unmodified-Since: true when the representation was not modified after the date. It does the job of If-Match when the client has no entity-tag, and is ignored if If-Match is present. If false the server MUST NOT perform the method.
  • If-Range: defined in RFC 7233. If its validator does not match, the server ignores the Range header and sends the whole new representation instead of a 412.
sections.eli5: These headers are the 'only if' words: only if it is the same, only if it is different, only if changed since, only if not changed since.

sections.title: The 304 and 412 Status Codes
sections.content:
304 Not Modified means a conditional GET or HEAD would have produced a 200 (OK) but the condition was false, so there is no need to send the data because the client already has a valid copy. The server MUST include the header fields it would have sent in a 200 response among Cache-Control, Content-Location, Date, ETag, Expires and Vary. A 304 response cannot contain a message body.

412 Precondition Failed means one or more conditions in the request headers were false when tested on the server. It lets a client prevent a method from being applied when the resource is in an unexpected state.
sections.eli5: 304 means 'you already have the latest, I will not resend it'. 412 means 'the thing changed, so I did not do what you asked'.

sections.title: Evaluation and Precedence
sections.content:
A server evaluates preconditions after its normal request checks and just before it would perform the method. It MUST ignore all preconditions if the response without them would not be a 2xx or 412. A server that is neither the origin server nor able to act as a cache for the target MUST NOT evaluate them and MUST forward them. They are also ignored for methods such as CONNECT, OPTIONS and TRACE.

When several are present they are evaluated in this order:

  1. If-Match, when the recipient is the origin server.
  2. If-Unmodified-Since, if If-Match is absent.
  3. If-None-Match, with 304 for GET or HEAD and 412 otherwise if false.
  4. If-Modified-Since for GET or HEAD, if If-None-Match is absent; 304 if false.
  5. If-Range for a GET with a Range header, giving 206 (Partial Content) when the validator matches.
  6. Otherwise all conditions are met and the action is performed.

The order exists because lost update checks are stricter than cache validation, a validated cache beats a partial response, and entity tags are presumed more accurate than dates.
sections.eli5: If several 'only if' rules are given, the server checks them in a fixed order, strictest first, and stops at the first one that fails.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Validators are not meant to ensure the validity of a representation, guard against malicious changes or detect man-in-the-middle attacks. At best they allow efficient cache updates and optimistic concurrent writes when everyone behaves nicely; at worst the condition fails and the client gets a response no more harmful than a normal exchange.

Entity-tags can also cause privacy risks. A site could construct a tag unique to a user, send it in a cacheable response with a long freshness time, and read it back in later conditional requests to re-identify the user. User agents ought to clear or replace their cache when the user does privacy-maintaining actions such as clearing cookies or switching to private browsing.
sections.eli5: These version stickers are for saving time, not for catching cheaters. A sneaky site could even give you a unique sticker to recognize you later, so clearing your cache helps.

messages.note: Sends the entity-tag it stored earlier.

messages.label: 304 Not Modified
messages.note: Tag still matches, so no body is sent.

items.title: If-Match
items.text: Proceed only if the tag matches (strong comparison).

items.title: If-None-Match
items.text: Proceed only if no tag matches (weak comparison).

items.title: If-Modified-Since
items.text: Proceed only if changed after the date.

items.title: If-Unmodified-Since
items.text: Proceed only if not changed after the date.

items.title: If-Range
items.text: Send the range if the validator matches, else the whole thing.
